  1. net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api

Style text from Java, Kotlin, Scala, or scripts

Register text styles and read formatted text contains complete examples for updating data and closing the resources your code creates.

Choose your addon’s language to create a text effect, give it a formatting name, and draw text using that name. Each example explains where the code runs and how to remove its registrations. The Java, Kotlin, Scala, Groovy, and ZenScript helpers share the same text implementation.

Calls used in the examples

Calls used in this guide
Call or settingArgumentsWhat it does
MovementRegistry.create(id, colorSpeed, moveSpeed, palette, animationSpeed, options)Effect ID; color/movement controls; RGB palette; playback multiplier; option mapChoose a built-in effect and its settings. Use the effect’s reference for supported option names and ranges.
ChromaticDefinitions.register(kind, id, trigger, color, effect)Entry kind; unique registration ID; text trigger; color/effectRegister the entry your text should select. Only supply the color or effect appropriate to that kind.
receipt.close()No argumentsRemove the entry installed by this receipt when your addon or script no longer needs it.
colorSpeed / moveSpeedFinite effect-specific controlsAdjust the selected effect’s color and movement behavior. Geometry settings remain independent of playback speed.
animationSpeedFinite multiplier from -32 to 32Change playback speed; a negative value reverses time and zero freezes it.
optionsMap of supported setting names to valuesOverride matching keys in the effect descriptor. Unsupported names and invalid ranges are rejected.

When you finish: Creating an effect does not register a text trigger. Retain the receipt through the tool/script lifetime and close it during teardown. Parsing and registration do not need a screen; calls to Minecraft’s font renderer run on the client thread.

Where the code runs and who removes it

Java and Kotlin use the mod’s normal runtime, including Forgelin. Scala helpers need Scalar for Scala 3; Scalar Legacy supplies a different language version. Install GroovyScript or CraftTweaker only for scripts using it. Kotlin, Groovy and Scala can also call the Java methods directly; ZenScript uses mods.chromaticcodes.Text. Ordinary scripts run at startup. A GroovyScript reload checks the script’s complete set of definitions and applies them together, keeping the previous set on failure. Creating or inspecting text data can run without a client screen; calls to FontRenderer belong on the client thread.

Choose Scala effect settings with named methods

Common effect settings have typed names as well as the flexible option method. Both paths create a new immutable description and run the same Java schema validation when you call build(). They do not change a registered effect in place.

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.scaladsl.Chromatic.*
// Before: effect("wave", 0xFFCC00).option("amplitudeY", 2.5).option("opacity", 0.7)
val wave = effect("wave", 0xFFCC00).amplitudeY(2.5).opacity(0.7).primaryColor(0xFF8800)
val callback = wave.build()

Opacity is a fraction from 0 to 1; vertical amplitude is in GUI pixels; primary color is RGB from 0 to 0xFFFFFF. Unsupported options and invalid ranges still fail normally. Keep option(name, value) for other settings. Kotlin already accepts ordinary List/Map values and named defaults, while Groovy uses normal maps and closures. Their existing syntax needs no duplicate options model.

Configure an effect

This creates a wave effect with the supplied colors and vertical amplitude, then sets its playback speed independently. Each language produces the same effect. Creating it alone does not give text a code to use; register a name for it in the next example.

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.MovementRegistry;
var effect = MovementRegistry.create("wave", 1, 1,
    java.util.List.of(0xFF4000, 0xFFD000), 0.5f,
    java.util.Map.of("amplitudeY", 2.5));

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.*
val effect = textEffect("wave", listOf(0xFF4000, 0xFFD000),
    playbackSpeed = 0.5f, options = mapOf("amplitudeY" to 2.5))

def text = mods.chromatic_codes.text
def effect = text.effect('wave', [0xFF4000, 0xFFD000],
    1f, 1f, 0.5f, [amplitudeY: 2.5d])

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.scaladsl.Chromatic.*
val effect = net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.scaladsl.Chromatic.effect("wave", 0xFF4000, 0xFFD000)
  .option("amplitudeY", 2.5).speed(0.5f).build()

import mods.chromaticcodes.Text;
val effect = Text.effect("wave", [0xFF4000, 0xFFD000])
    .option("amplitudeY", 2.5).speed(0.5);

The selected effect checks these settings when it is created. Playback speed changes how fast time advances through the animation; it does not change the wave’s height or letter spacing. The meanings of the other speed controls depend on the effect. Built-in effect types are ready after mod construction; register a custom type before trying to create it.

Register a text code and remove it later

This registers a gold color and a wave effect under names your text can use. Choose IDs in your mod’s namespace and keep the returned registration objects. Call close() later when removing those entries, not immediately after setup. Groovy replaces its previous script registrations after a successful reload; CraftTweaker records the changes as startup actions.

import net.minecraft.util.ResourceLocation;
import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.ChromaticDefinitions;
var receipt = ChromaticDefinitions.register(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.EFFECT_NAME,
    new ResourceLocation("my_mod", "warm_wave"), "warm_wave", null, effect);
// Later, when your contribution unloads:
receipt.close();

import net.minecraft.util.ResourceLocation
val receipt = effectCode(ResourceLocation("my_mod", "warm_wave"), "warm_wave", effect)
// Later, when your contribution unloads:
receipt.close()

// In the reloadable script loader; do not manually call lifecycle hooks:
text.namedEffect('my_pack:warm_wave', 'warm_wave', effect)
text.color('my_pack:gold', 'gold', 0xFFCC00)
// Omitting these declarations from a successful reload removes this owner's entries.

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.scaladsl.Chromatic.*
val codes = definitions("my_mod") { text =>
  text.effect("warm_wave", effect)
  text.color("gold", 0xFFCC00)
}
// Later, on contribution unload:
codes.close()

Text.namedEffect("my_pack:warm_wave", "warm_wave", effect);
Text.color("my_pack:gold", "gold", 0xFFCC00);
// Explicitly remove only this facade's still-current contribution:
Text.remove("my_pack:warm_wave");

Closing a registration removes only the exact entry it installed. If another registration has replaced it, closing the older object leaves the new entry in place. Removing the replacement does not restore the displaced entry. A short try-with-resources or Kotlin use block around setup would remove your code as soon as that block ends.

Choose how text refers to a color or effect

Choose a short character code such as &z, a readable name such as &[gold], or an effect object used directly by your code. The examples register each kind. Character and named colors, effects, and outlines are separate entry categories.

var color = ChromaticDefinitions.register(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.COLOR_CHAR,
    new ResourceLocation("my_mod", "gold_char"), 'Z', 0xFFCC00, null);
var direct = ChromaticDefinitions.register(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.EFFECT,
    new ResourceLocation("my_mod", "direct_wave"), null, null, effect);
// Retain both receipts until unload.

val color = formattingCode(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.COLOR_CHAR,
    ResourceLocation("my_mod", "gold_char"), trigger = 'Z', rgb = 0xFFCC00)
val direct = formattingCode(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.EFFECT,
    ResourceLocation("my_mod", "direct_wave"), effect = effect)

text.characterColor('my_pack:gold_char', 'Z', 0xFFCC00)
text.characterEffect('my_pack:wave_char', 'Y', effect)
text.characterOutline('my_pack:outline_char', 'X')
text.directEffect('my_pack:direct_wave', effect)

val codes = definitions("my_mod") { text =>
  text.code(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.COLOR_CHAR, "gold_char", Char.box('Z'), Int.box(0xFFCC00))
  text.code(ChromaticDefinitions.Kind.EFFECT, "direct_wave", null, callback = effect)
}

Text.characterColor("my_pack:gold_char", "Z", 0xFFCC00);
Text.characterEffect("my_pack:wave_char", "Y", effect);
Text.characterOutline("my_pack:outline_char", "X");
Text.directEffect("my_pack:direct_wave", effect);

The registry’s current case-sensitivity rules apply. Character inputs must contain exactly one UTF-16 character; do not use a surrogate-pair emoji as a character trigger. Kotlin/Scala callers can also use one atomic Java editor block for dependent changes.

Measure formatted text and fit it into a line

The example measures formatted text, wraps it into lines, and trims it to a chosen width. Supply a function returning each character’s ordinary width in your font. The example’s constant width of six only demonstrates the calls; Minecraft’s usual font gives different letters different widths.

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.ChromaticText;
var layout = ChromaticText.compile("&[gold]ABC");
float width = layout.width(character -> 6);
String clipped = layout.trim(12, false, character -> 6);
String wrapped = layout.wrap(12, character -> 6);
var first = layout.glyphs().getFirst();
String visible = layout.plain();

val layout = ChromaticText.compile("&[gold]ABC")
val width = layout.width { 6 }
val clipped = layout.trim(12, false) { 6 }
val wrapped = layout.wrap(12) { 6 }
val first = layout.glyphs().first()
val visible = layout.plain()

def layout = text.compile('&[gold]ABC')
def width = layout.width({ c -> 6 } as java.util.function.ToIntFunction)
def clipped = layout.trim(12, false, { c -> 6 } as java.util.function.ToIntFunction)
def wrapped = layout.wrap(12, { c -> 6 } as java.util.function.ToIntFunction)
def first = layout.glyphs().getFirst()
def visible = layout.plain()

val layout = net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.ChromaticText.compile("&[gold]ABC")
val width = layout.width(_ => 6)
val clipped = layout.trim(12, false, _ => 6)
val wrapped = layout.wrap(12, _ => 6)
val first = layout.glyphs().getFirst()
val visible = layout.plain()

val layout = Text.compile("&[gold]ABC");
val width = layout.width(function(character) { return 6; });
val clipped = layout.trim(12, false, function(character) { return 6; });
val wrapped = layout.wrap(12, function(character) { return 6; });
val first = layout.glyph(0);
val rgb = layout.color(0);
val visible = layout.plain();

Glyphs retain complete visible Unicode text and raw UTF-16 start/end offsets. The width callback receives one UTF-16 code unit, matching the Java parser contract. Effects and bold flags affect measured advance. Continuation prefixes use the existing parser’s reconstruction rules; see the syntax guide for mixed color/effect limitations. Custom colors/outlines return -1 when absent in the ZenScript layout.

Write a function that colors text red

This custom callback keeps position and size unchanged and supplies a fixed red foreground. Replace the sample expression with your own animation while retaining finite output.

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.IChromaticEffect;
IChromaticEffect custom = new IChromaticEffect() {
    @Override public int getRenderColor(int original, float x, float y) { return 0xFF0000; }
    @Override public float getXOffset(float x, float y) { return 0; }
    @Override public float getYOffset(float x, float y) { return 0; }
};

val custom = object : IChromaticEffect {
    override fun getRenderColor(original: Int, x: Float, y: Float) = 0xFF0000
    override fun getXOffset(x: Float, y: Float) = 0f
    override fun getYOffset(x: Float, y: Float) = 0f
}

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.IChromaticEffect
def custom = [
    getRenderColor: { int original, float x, float y -> 0xFF0000 },
    getXOffset: { float x, float y -> 0f },
    getYOffset: { float x, float y -> 0f }
] as IChromaticEffect

val custom = new net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.IChromaticEffect:
  override def getRenderColor(original: Int, x: Float, y: Float): Int = 0xFF0000
  override def getXOffset(x: Float, y: Float): Float = 0f
  override def getYOffset(x: Float, y: Float): Float = 0f

val custom = Text.custom(function(channel, x, y, original, fallback, milliseconds) {
    if (channel == "color") return 16711680.0;
    return fallback;
});
Text.namedEffect("my_pack:red", "red", custom);

ZenScript channels cover color, x/y offsets, opacity, uniform and axis scales, outline/color, static/animated classifications, horizontal blending, passthrough and whole-segment transforms. Return fallback for channels you do not change. Generic callbacks cannot manufacture the concrete volumetric layer geometry; use the registered 3d preset for that. The script callback is shared by reference and may be sampled by common-side layout code, so keep it free of client-only assumptions and registry mutation.

Preview an animation at a fixed time

The example samples the animation at a chosen time, making screenshots or comparisons repeatable. The temporary clock setting applies only to the calling thread and is restored when the block returns or throws. Playback speed still multiplies the time seen by the effect.

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.TextEffectClock;
try (var sample = TextEffectClock.at(250.0)) {
    int rgb = effect.getRenderColor(0xFFFFFF, 10, 20);
}

atEffectTime(250.0) {
    val rgb = effect.getRenderColor(0xFFFFFF, 10f, 20f)
}

import net.phoenix.chromatic_codes.api.TextEffectClock
def sample = TextEffectClock.at(250d)
try { def rgb = effect.getRenderColor(0xFFFFFF, 10f, 20f) }
finally { sample.close() }

atTime(250.0) {
  val rgb = effect.getRenderColor(0xFFFFFF, 10f, 20f)
}

Text.atTime(250.0, function() {
    val width = Text.compile("&[warm_wave]ABC").width(function(character) { return 6; });
    print(width);
});

Keep the work synchronous and on the same thread. A clock scope does not make arbitrary mutable callbacks thread-safe. Layout-only sampling does not allocate GPU resources.

Draw through Minecraft’s font renderer

Call from an actual screen’s client render callback. Kotlin, Groovy and Scala use the same Java renderer. ZenScript can provide styled strings to another mod’s exposed GUI renderer, such as Offscreen’s draw callback.

net.minecraft.client.Minecraft.getMinecraft().fontRenderer
    .drawString("&[warm_wave]Hello", 12, 12, 0xFFFFFF);

net.minecraft.client.Minecraft.getMinecraft().fontRenderer
    .drawString("&[warm_wave]Hello", 12, 12, 0xFFFFFF)

net.minecraft.client.Minecraft.getMinecraft().fontRenderer
    .drawString('&[warm_wave]Hello', 12, 12, 0xFFFFFF)

net.minecraft.client.Minecraft.getMinecraft().fontRenderer
  .drawString("&[warm_wave]Hello", 12, 12, 0xFFFFFF)

// Requires OffscreenCleanroom too; declare this in a client-side script.
import mods.offscreencleanroom.Windows;
val panel = Windows.screen("Styled text", 640, 480);
panel.on("draw", function(event) {
    event.text("&[warm_wave]Hello", 12, 12, -1, true);
    return false;
});
// Open panel from your GUI/input action, not during startup script loading.

The formatting code must still be registered when drawing. Other renderers may bypass Minecraft’s font hooks, and input fields may strip formatting tokens. Chromatic Codes does not open its own GUI from a common-side script.
